title: But what is a Neural Network? | Chapter 1, Deep learning
hook: A sloppy 28×28 pixel '3' appears on screen and the narration dares the viewer to explain why recognizing it is trivially easy for humans yet dauntingly hard to program.

scenes.purpose: Establish the core tension between human effortlessness and computational difficulty

on_screen.desc: Large pixelated '3' rendered as a grid of colored squares
Brace labels showing 28px × 28px dimensions
Pi creature reacting with 'sassy' then 'pondering' expression
Arrow from pixel grid pointing to handwritten '3' symbol

scenes.transition: Multiple alternate '3' images fade in on the right; pixel grid gains yellow tint to show firing cells concept
scenes.narration_gist: Your brain trivially recognizes wildly different pixel patterns as the same digit, but writing a program to do this goes from comically trivial to dauntingly difficult.

scenes.purpose: State the video's scope and promise: structure now, learning next

on_screen.desc: Words 'Machine learning' (green) and 'Neural network' (blue)
Small network diagram with layered circles and edges
Equation σ(W_l · a_l + b_l) written above network
Two video-icon placeholders labeled 'Structure' and 'Learning'

scenes.transition: Teacher-student scene; network diagram shrinks into video thumbnail icons
scenes.narration_gist: I want to show you what a neural network actually is as a piece of math, not a buzzword — structure in this video, learning in the next.

scenes.purpose: Introduce neurons as number-holders and show the full layered architecture

on_screen.desc: 784-neuron input layer with brace labeled '784'
Full network: input → two 16-neuron hidden layers → 10-neuron output
Output labels 0–9 next to output neurons
Label 'Activation' with yellow highlight on example neuron showing decimal 0.2

scenes.transition: Pixel grid of a digit morphs into the first layer of circles; hidden layers fade in with large '?' marks
scenes.narration_gist: Each neuron holds a number called its activation; 784 input neurons encode pixel brightness, two hidden layers of 16 are a mystery for now, and 10 output neurons represent digit confidence.

scenes.purpose: Motivate the layered structure with a hierarchy of visual abstractions

on_screen.desc: Handwritten digit images for 9, 8, 4 with colored overlays
Equations: nine = upper_loop + right_line, eight = upper_loop + lower_loop
Network diagram with second-to-last layer neurons next to sub-pattern images
Yellow edge group flashing between pattern layer and output layer

scenes.transition: Equation components fly into position beside network layer neurons; earlier digit equations fade out
scenes.narration_gist: Ideally each hidden layer detects increasingly abstract sub-components — edges → loops/lines → digit parts — so the final layer just combines these patterns.

scenes.purpose: Zoom into one neuron to explain how weights encode a pixel detector

on_screen.desc: Single enlarged neuron with incoming weighted edges (green/red thickness)
28×28 pixel grid showing green positive weights and red negative weights
Question 'What parameters should exist?' in green
Weighted sum expression w1·a1 + w2·a2 + … + wn·an

scenes.transition: Decimal parameter list transforms into a colored weight grid aligned with the pixel region
scenes.narration_gist: Assign a weight to every connection; a weighted sum of pixel activations detects a region when positive weights sit on the target pixels and negative weights surround them.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the sigmoid (bias) to squish weighted sums into [0,1] and add thresholding

on_screen.desc: Sigmoid / logistic curve plotted from negative to positive inputs
Expression sigmoid(w·a + bias) with bias highlighted
Labels 'weights → what pattern' and 'bias → when to activate'
Running total '13,000 weights and biases' count

scenes.transition: Sigmoid plot fades; attention shifts to scale of parameters across all layers
scenes.narration_gist: Pump the weighted sum through a sigmoid to get a value in [0,1], and add a bias to set the threshold at which the neuron turns on.

scenes.purpose: Compress the full computation into compact matrix-vector notation

on_screen.desc: Matrix equation a_{l+1} = σ(W_l · a_l + b_l) with color-coded vectors
Column vector of activations a_l (green)
Weight matrix W_l with rows = next-layer neurons
Bias vector b_l added before sigmoid wraps everything

scenes.transition: Verbose per-neuron formula is replaced by the single matrix equation; earlier weight grid fades
scenes.narration_gist: Organize activations as a vector, weights as a matrix, biases as a vector — then one compact expression σ(Wa + b) describes every layer transition.

scenes.purpose: Reframe the entire network as one large, concrete mathematical function

on_screen.desc: Statement 'The network is a function: 784 inputs → 10 outputs'
Full MNIST network diagram with activations lit up for a real digit
Parameter count '~13,000 weights and biases'
Highlighted winning output neuron with surrounding rectangle

scenes.transition: Network demo runs live feed-forward pass; output neuron lights up and gets a bounding box
scenes.narration_gist: The whole network is just one complicated function with 13,000 parameters — reassuringly complex, but still just a function — and learning means finding the right parameter values.

scenes.purpose: Honest postscript: sigmoid is old-school; ReLU is what modern nets use

on_screen.desc: Interview framing text naming guest Lisha Li
ReLU curve: max(0, a) — flat at zero then linear
Label 'ReLU = Rectified Linear Unit'
Contrast note: sigmoid ↔ ReLU ease of training

scenes.transition: Talking-head style cut; Manim animation of ReLU shape replaces sigmoid plot
scenes.narration_gist: Early networks used sigmoid, but modern deep networks almost always use ReLU — it's simpler and much easier to train.

lessons: Open with a concrete, familiar object and a paradox that makes the viewer feel the problem viscerally before any formalism appears.
Use a recurring visual object (the network diagram) as an anchor that returns in every scene so viewers track cumulative progress.
Introduce abstraction in stages: show the messy per-neuron case first, then reveal the compact matrix form as a reward for following along.
Place color-coded weight grids spatially aligned with the pixel region they describe so the visual and the concept are inseparable.
Signal scope explicitly on screen — 'this video covers structure, the next covers learning' — so viewers know exactly what the current episode promises.
End with a credibility-building twist (ReLU over sigmoid) that shows honest nuance without undermining the lesson just taught.
